units: the writer explains what got her out of bed so early
an observing club had flagged the passing of a celestial body
the clear sky decided her to take her telescope along
she drove for a good while before reaching the spot
the planet passed very close to the lunar disc and was then hidden
the steady air made the image very sharp
she made out detail she cannot reach from home
the cold delayed the settling of the instrument to the outside temperature
she invites the person she writes to to come with her the following night
text: You wanted to know what dragged me out of bed before dawn, so here is the whole story. The observing club had flagged a very close passing, and since the sky looked like staying clear, I loaded the telescope into the back of the car. Three quarters of an hour of driving, frozen fingers, and what a sight it was. The planet skimmed the edge of the lunar disc, then went behind it all at once, with no fading. The air was so steady that the image barely shivered, and I picked out detail that I never manage to get from my own balcony. The night being bitter, the tube took an age to settle to the outside air, so I spent a long stretch stamping about and breathing into my gloves. Now I understand what the old observers meant. Come out with me tomorrow night, and you will see the difference straight away.

units: the interview deals with the crowding of the near orbits
craft that have stopped working keep circling the globe after their mission ends
a collision throws off a swarm of fragments
a tiny strike can pierce a tank
a tiny strike can tear off a receiving element
the specialist recommends a planned descent designed in from the outset
she also proposes catching the debris already up there with a net or a harpoon
the debris caught would be steered towards a controlled fall into the sea
she judges the solution workable only if the operators take up one common rule
text: Should we be alarmed at how crowded the low orbits have become? The engineer we spoke to answers without hedging: craft that have stopped working carry on circling above our heads long after their working life has ended, and every knock throws off a swarm of fragments. What does a working satellite risk? A tiny strike is enough to pierce a tank or tear an aerial away. Her remedy? First a planned descent, paid for and designed in while the craft is still being drawn up. Then a clear out of what is already up there, debris caught in a net or on a harpoon and steered down to a safe fall into the sea. Is that workable? She believes so, provided that the operators take up one common rule and hold to it. With no shared constraint, she says, each operator pushes the cost onto the next one.

units: the keeper of the dome asks the narrator which he prefers, watching directly or recording
the narrator admits he cannot choose
she describes the human gaze as a brief act that leaves no trace
she describes the recording device as a tool that piles up moments
this piling up brings out what is too faint for the eye
the narrator objects that a drawing keeps something of the feeling
she grants that a sketch holds the memory of an evening
she states that a bare image tells nothing on its own
she concludes that photographing means handing your memory over
text: The woman who looks after the dome asked me which of the two I preferred, the eye or the sensor. I told her that I had never managed to choose between them. So she set the pair of them side by side for me. The eye, she said, takes hold of a moment the way a hand takes hold of a pebble, fast and leaving nothing behind; the sensor waits, gathers, piles moment upon moment until whatever is very faint rises slowly into view. I objected that an observer's drawing holds a warmth no machine can give. She smiled and granted me that much: a sketch carries a whole evening in it, while a bare image carries nothing at all. Then came the line I have kept. Looking is remembering with your eyes; photographing is handing your memory to a device. We stayed under the open slit until the cold drove us out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the history of sky watching falls into families of instruments
the earliest tools rested on measuring angles by naked sight
those tools leaned on tables copied out by hand
the lens telescope came next
the lens telescope suffers from a fault of colour
the mirror removed that fault but makes the instrument heavier
the mirror made very wide apertures possible
the sensitive plate gave access to bodies invisible to the eye
electronic sensors and aerials carried observation beyond the visible
each family of instruments inherited the methods of the one before
text: The story of sky watching falls neatly enough into families of instruments. The earliest of them measured angles by naked sight alone and leaned on tables copied out by hand, generation after generation. Then came the telescope built round lenses, which shut the gaze inside a closed tube but never shook off a stubborn fringe of colour. Then the mirror, heavier to carry, free of that fringe, and open to apertures that ground glass could never reach. Then the sensitive plate, able to probe bodies far too faint for the retina. Then, last of all, electronic sensors and linked arrays of aerials, which carried observation clean out of the visible range. None of these families drove out the one before it. Each inherited its ways of measuring, its catalogues and, more often than not, its mistakes.

units: a star forms from a cloud of cold gas that gives way
the drawing in heats the centre until fusion starts
fusion halts the collapse of the cloud
there follows a long settled period of steady burning of the fuel
the fuel running out swells the envelope and cools the surface
the outer layers drift apart and seed the medium with heavy elements
a dense core is left at the centre and cools without end
the heaviest bodies close with an explosion
the blast of that explosion squeezes the clouds nearby and sets off new births there
text: A star begins its life in a cloud of cold gas that gives way under its own weight. As the cloud draws in, its heart grows hotter and hotter, until fusion takes hold and the collapse is halted. There follows a long and settled stretch of life, during which the star burns through its fuel at a steady rate. Once that store starts to run low, the envelope swells out of all proportion and the surface cools; the star turns into a reddish giant. Its outer layers drift away in the end, seeding the medium around them with heavy elements. At the centre nothing is left but a dense, scorching core, which cools from then on without ever having done. The heaviest stars take a far more violent road and close with an explosion whose blast squeezes the clouds nearby, where fresh stars will be born.

units: an amateur left his listening station recording while he was away
a power cut threw the clock of the station out
the files stacked up with no date to go by
the amateur nearly deleted the lot
he opened the last file and heard a short signal that kept returning
he passed the trace on to a university observatory
a researcher there picked out an onboard transmitter that had been taken for dead
that craft spoke only when its panels caught the sunlight at one precise angle
the faulty clock had shifted the listening into the one favourable window
text: An amateur radio listener had got into the way of leaving his station to record on its own while he was away. A power cut threw the clock out, so the files stacked up with no date to go by, and he came close to erasing them all. Out of plain curiosity he opened the last one of them anyway, and found a short signal returning at even intervals. Since that beat meant nothing to him, he passed the trace on to a university observatory. There a researcher recognised the signature of an onboard transmitter that everyone had taken for dead an age ago. Starved of power, the craft spoke only when its panels caught the sunlight at one precise angle. The faulty clock, by shifting every listening session, had dropped the recording into the single window in which the object had anything to say.

units: soft images come most often from the setting of the mirrors and not from the sky
the instrument must go outside half an hour before observing
the heat held inside the tube spoils the image
the eyepiece is swapped for a pierced cap to check the centring
through that cap you should see circles nested one inside another
an off centre is put right with the screws of the bottom mirror
the screws must never be tightened right down
you then aim at a bright star and throw it out of focus to get a ring
an uneven ring is corrected by an eighth of a turn of the screw concerned
text: The instrument you have just bought is giving you soft, mushy images and you are beginning to lose patience? Nine times out of ten the mirrors are out of line, not the sky. Here is the drill to follow. Carry the thing outside a good half hour before you aim at anything, or the heat shut inside the tube will smear the lot. Take the eyepiece out, drop a pierced cap in its place and look through: you should see a set of neatly nested circles. If the centre sits off to one side, work on the bottom mirror with the screws behind it, a shade at a time, and never tighten one right down. Put the eyepiece back, aim at a bright star and throw it slightly out of focus, and you get a ring. That ring should look even all the way round. If it bulges on one side, turn the matching screw an eighth of a turn, no more.

units: a new receiving array is going up on a dry plateau
the engineers set this site against an observatory placed outside the atmosphere
the two installations look at the same bodies
the one on the ground can be lengthened and mended part by part
the craft in orbit has to work with nobody to touch it
the one on the ground is hampered by air that muddles the signals
the craft in orbit has vacuum in front of its shell
the one on the ground has power in plenty
the craft in orbit has to save every scrap of energy
those in charge hold that the two approaches complete each other
text: On the dry plateau where the latest receiving array is going up, the engineers like to set their site against an observatory lofted clear of the atmosphere. Both of them look at the same bodies, and there the likeness comes to an end. The array on the ground can be lengthened, mended, swapped part by part; the craft in orbit has to work first time, since no technician is going up there to tighten a bolt. The one on the ground is troubled by air that muddles the signals; the other has nothing but vacuum in front of its shell. The ground station, on the other hand, draws all the power it wants, while its rival counts every last scrap of energy. The team running the site are sure the two approaches complete each other: one keeps the long watches, the other catches what the air hides from us.

units: seen from the road the dome looks like a pale pebble laid on a ridge
its open slit lets in a draught of icy air
the bare concrete floor inside throws back the sound of footsteps
the tube of the instrument leans towards the opening
the tube swings round with a low unbroken sound
wooden drawers hold coloured filters and wrapped eyepieces
an electrical panel blinks above the drawers
the sky outside is free of haze
you can pick out a milky trail, a low reddish body and a satellite crossing the field
text: From the road that climbs towards it, the dome looks like a pale pebble laid on the ridge. Its slit opens like an eyelid and lets in a draught of icy air. Inside, the bare grey concrete throws every footstep back at you. The tube of the instrument, huge, leans towards the opening and swings round with a low, unbroken drone. Along the wall stand wooden drawers where coloured filters lie sleeping, with eyepieces wrapped in cloth and cable coiled and tied off with leather. Above them an electrical panel blinks at long, uneven intervals. Outside, the night spreads without a shred of haze: you can pick out the milky trail crossing the vault, a reddish body sitting low over the horizon, and the thread of a satellite drifting from one edge of the field to the other, in silence.

units: at first the sky surveys belonged to the team that had taken them
that claim shocked nobody because instruments were scarce
digital sensors turned out volumes of measurement no single team could handle
open archives took hold because of those volumes
the difficulty now lies in sifting the data rather than gathering it
the writer holds that paying for an instrument without paying for the use of its data makes no sense
he asks that a fixed share of every programme go to archiving
he also asks for funding of calibration and of public tools of analysis
without that the measurements heaped up will never be put to use
text: The case is worth retelling in the order it grew. At the outset, sky surveys belonged to the team that had taken them, and nobody thought that odd: plates were scarce and instruments scarcer still. Then digital sensors began pouring out volumes of measurement that no single team could work through, and open archives settled the matter on their own. Now comes the present stage, where the hard part is no longer gathering but sifting. My position fits in one sentence: paying for an instrument without paying for the use of its data is like sinking a well and forgetting the bucket. Agencies ought therefore to set aside a fixed share of every programme for archiving, for calibration and for public tools of analysis. Otherwise we shall heap up measurements that nobody ever goes down to look at.
